segments.text: Il custode risponde al suo telefono. «Ho appena finito un lavoro. Ora arrivo», spiega al signore del trasporto. Paolo guarda la porta gialla, ancora chiusa a chiave. Ada tiene la busta; Elena tiene le foto tra i due fogli. Il signore non chiede altri euro: aspetta e guarda le cinque scatole nel suo foglio. Sono le scatole uno, due, tre, quattro e cinque.

grammar.title: Grammatica
grammar.rule: ho controllato; hai controllato; ha controllato; abbiamo visitato; avete visitato; hanno scaricato
grammar.note_en:
The passato prossimo is a compound past tense: in this chapter it combines a present-tense form of avere, “have”, with a past participle, the verb form that names the completed action. The action belongs to an earlier time, but its completion matters now: a job has been checked, a table has been moved, or the cabinet has been loaded but its papers have not been inspected. Yesterday’s list and the present problem are connected by those completed actions. The tense is built by the verb forms, not by a time word alone.

The rule and first table give the attested auxiliary patterns. An auxiliary is a helping verb used to build a verb construction. Io ho controllato means “I have checked”; tu hai controllato means “you have checked”, for one familiar person; Elena ha controllato means “Elena has checked”; noi abbiamo visitato means “we have visited”; voi avete visitato means “you have visited”, addressed to more than one person; due persone hanno scaricato means “two people have unloaded”. Persona / Forma means “person / form”. Avere changes with the subject. In the displayed examples the participle does not change merely because the subject changes gender or number. This chapter does not claim a general rule for every construction with a preceding object pronoun; it teaches these attested patterns.

The second table isolates participles from the story. Controllato means “checked”; ho controllato means “I have checked”. Spostato means “moved”; ha spostato means “he has moved”. Caricato means “loaded”; abbiamo caricato means “we have loaded”. Scaricato means “unloaded”; hanno scaricato means “they have unloaded”. Scritto means “written”; ha scritto means “he has written”. Letto means “read”, as a completed action; hai letto means “you have read”. Forma, the caption, means “form”. Regular -are verbs form this participle with -ato: visitare → visitato, “visit → visited”. The first four table entries show this -ato ending. Regular -ire verbs use -ito: finire → finito, “finish → finished”. Finito, “finished”, shows that ending; the story uses it in the completed-job report. The last two are irregular forms of the familiar writing and reading verbs; learn the forms demonstrated, rather than inventing an -ato form for every verb. The masculine noun letto, “bed”, is already familiar, but it is not the reading in the completed-action phrase hai letto.

A question uses the same auxiliary and participle pattern. Lei ha scritto questo elenco? means “Have you written this list?”, addressed formally to the custodian. The Italian verb has the third-singular form ha with formal Lei, even though English translates it as “you have”. Hai controllato anche il numero tredici? means “Have you also checked number thirteen?”, addressed familiarly to Elena. Non ho mai visitato questa stanza means “I have never visited this room”. In the negative experience examples, non ... mai means “never”; non ho mai letto i fogli means “I have never read the papers”. Già means “already”, and appena means “just” in the sense of very recently. Ho appena finito un lavoro means “I have just finished a job”. These words refine the timing or experience; they do not by themselves create a past tense.

Ieri means “yesterday”: the previous cycle before today, which is Friday in the story. Undici, dodici and tredici mean eleven, twelve and thirteen: 11,12 and13. They are job labels on the custodian’s work list, not new box numbers. The original nine boxes still have labels1–9, and only boxes1–5 plus the shelf belong to the agreed thirty-euro transport. The missing signature shows an unfinished inspection; an empty room does not prove that the papers have been checked. Past loading and a present empty room can both be true while that task remains undone.
